How do people find their way, and their books, in a five-storey home turned public library?

"Which floor is the library?"

Role

UX Researcher · Deepanshi Nagarwal

Timeline

3 weeks of fieldwork

Methods

Observation, interviews, contextual inquiry, photo study

Site

Arthshila Ahmedabad, by BandukSmith Studio (2021)

the short version

A beautiful building that keeps its map a secret.

Arthshila's five-storey steel bookshelf is the soul of the building. Everyone looks up at it, photographs it and orients by it. Yet the same architecture that makes people wander makes it hard to find: floors aren't legible from the stairs, the collection has no catalogue, and events are announced everywhere except inside the building.

I mapped how visitors move, sit and search across all five floors, synthesised 10 insights, and proposed four light-touch interventions that add clarity without breaking the calm, house-like feel people love.

01 · context

From family home to public library.

Built as a residence in 2014 and transformed in 2021, Arthshila sits in Ahmedabad's institutional belt beside CEPT, IIM-A and Gujarat University. It is a multi-arts centre with a library, gallery, cinema and amphitheatre stacked on a footprint smaller than a tennis court.

02 · design process

Six steps, one staircase.

A mixed-methods approach paired what people do (behaviour mapping) with what they say and feel (interviews, think-aloud), triangulated against secondary research and comparable spaces like Conflictorium.

1

Discover

Literature on library UX, wayfinding and adaptive reuse; the architect's documentation.

2

Observe

15 timed sweeps across mornings, afternoons, evenings, weekdays and weekends.

3

Listen

18 semi-structured interviews and 6 think-aloud contextual inquiries.

4

Synthesise

Behaviour maps, empathy map, personas, five emerging patterns.

5

Define

10 insights, 4 major and 4 minor problems with root causes.

6

Design

4 opportunity areas with concepts and projected impact.

Research questions

  1. Navigation: how do people orient across five vertical levels?
  2. Behaviour: what do they do, where, and for how long?
  3. Discovery: how do they find books, films and digital resources?
  4. Experience: what drives comfort, satisfaction and return visits?
  5. Opportunity: where can design remove friction?

04 · time spent

Hours for some, minutes for others.

Dwell time splits visitors into two mindsets: efficiency-seekers who stay for hours and know where they're going, and explorers who drift through in under 90 minutes. The building currently serves explorers far better.

08 · patterns

Five tensions in one tower.

1

Architectural drama vs spatial legibility

The bookshelf is a brilliant anchor ("I'm on the side facing the bookshelf"), but beauty was prioritised over finding specific things.

2

Floors zone themselves

With almost no explicit zoning, people still matched floors to intent. The architecture already communicates character, so signage only needs to confirm it.

3

Discovery vs efficiency

Explorers love serendipity; regulars want speed. Today's design rewards the first and taxes the second.

4

The accessibility paradox

Free and physically open, yet cognitively closed. Minimal interpretation and a design-insider identity quietly signal "not for me" to newcomers.

5

Programming builds community

Events turn a study utility into a shared cultural platform, and they're the least visible thing in the building.

09 · key insights

Ten things the building told me.

01

Wayfinding is a systemic gap, not user error

Evidence · most first-timers asked for directions within 2 minutes; stair labels go unseen.

So · entry directory, progressive floor signage, an entrance kiosk.

02

Verticality brings discovery and navigation cost

Evidence · people enjoy the "treasure hunt" but over-explore (3.2 floors).

So · progressive disclosure: just enough info at the entry and landings.

03

Time is invisible

Evidence · visitors learn about events after arriving, often via Instagram mid-visit.

So · a "Today at Arthshila" now/next view at the entrance.

04

No catalogue forces browse-only use

Evidence · researchers spend 15-30 min hunting known titles; staff act as a human catalogue.

So · a minimal searchable catalogue near the library and desk.

05

Open acoustics undermine focus

Evidence · headphones come out and people relocate during events.

So · label silent, quiet and active floors; time events; add light acoustic treatment.

06

Workspaces don't fit research work

Evidence · materials spread on floors and sills; long sessions get uncomfortable.

So · larger tables with power and task lighting on floors 3 and 4.

07

Serendipity is the core value

Evidence · nearly everyone mentions a happy surprise: a book, an artwork, a person.

So · guide, don't over-script; keep open browsing paths.

08

It's a "third place"

Evidence · regulars treat it as a social and intellectual home.

So · protect informality while giving newcomers a map in.

09

Event info is fragmented

Evidence · split across Instagram, website and word of mouth; people miss events.

So · one source of truth feeding the board, Instagram, WhatsApp and calendar.

10

Analog by choice, digital by need

Evidence · professionals deliberately leave laptops; people love the calm, non-commercial vibe.

So · one or two focused digital touchpoints; keep the rest analog.

10 · problem framing

Where it hurts most.

Major problems

Resource discovery friction

No catalogue, no shelf labels, a non-standard system spread over floors. Result: 18 min per topic search.

First-visit wayfinding confusion

Minimal signage and an assumption that the layout is self-evident. Result: repeated questions and staff burden.

Programming awareness gap

Events promoted off-site, not in the building. Result: screenings and talks run below capacity.

An unused rooftop

No shade, seating or water in Ahmedabad heat. Result: the most-loved view sits idle most afternoons.

Minor problems

Upper shelves out of reach

Visible but unreachable books; part of the collection is effectively hidden.

Too few power outlets

Seat choice is dictated by sockets; sessions end when batteries do.

Dim interior zones

Fuels the window-seat scramble and shrinks effective capacity.

Invisible digital resources

Computers and databases used by just 5% of library users.

how might we...

help every visitor know what's on each floor, and what's on today, without breaking the quiet, house-like magic of Arthshila?

11 · solutions

Clarity, lightly.

Four interventions, each adding the minimum layer of information needed to remove friction while leaving discovery and calm intact.

● Opportunity 1

Hybrid catalogue

  • Searchable web catalogue showing each book's floor
  • Minimal bronze or laser-etched shelf section markers
  • Colour-coded spines by discipline
  • Touch kiosk near the entry to browse and map

● Opportunity 2

Layered wayfinding

  • Illustrated one-page floor map at the desk
  • Architecture-integrated signs at stair landings
  • "You are here" floor directory at the entry
  • Optional 5-minute staff orientation

● Opportunity 3

One programme channel

  • Events screen and printed board by the amphitheatre
  • Opt-in WhatsApp and email announcements
  • Desk staff mention what's on at check-in
  • QR codes linking to one calendar

● Opportunity 4

First-visit onboarding

  • Welcome card: map, collection, calendar, house rules
  • 2-minute desk script: "library on 3 and 4, gallery on 2..."
  • Optional first-timer badge to invite help
  • Numbered self-guided tour markers

12 · concepts

One colour per floor.

Tying wayfinding and the catalogue together: each floor gets a colour that appears on its landing sign, its shelf markers and the book spines, so a catalogue result like "Floor 3 · red" leads you straight there.

13 · reflection

What I'd do next.

Limitations

  • Three weeks can't capture semester breaks, festivals or monsoon.
  • Participants were self-selected; non-visitors are missing.
  • Visible observation may have nudged behaviour.
  • Interviews were in English and Hindi only.
  • Dwell times and paths were measured by hand, not sensors.

Next steps

  1. Prototype the orientation handout and floor directory; test with first-time visitors.
  2. Pilot the spreadsheet catalogue and measure search time against the 18-minute baseline.
  3. Run a monsoon and exam-season observation round.
  4. Recruit non-visitors from nearby campuses to understand who isn't coming in.
